 Timor-Leste Dengue Modeling Reveals Widespread Infection Risk and Sharp Coastal Hotspots
 by 
 November 16, 2026 
 in 
 Health 
 Reading Time: 5 mins read
 0 
 Timor-Leste Dengue Modeling Reveals Widespread Infection Risk and Sharp Coastal Hotspots
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 A nationwide, population-representative serosurvey conducted across Timor-Leste has revealed that dengue virus transmission is extensive across the country, showing pronounced spatial variation and severe hotspots of infection risk along northern and eastern coastal zones. By combining empirical age-stratified antibody detection with Bayesian sero-catalytic and geostatistical modeling, investigators established that the annual per-capita risk of dengue virus infection for a susceptible individual exceeded five percent across most geographic areas. The findings provide the first high-resolution, nationwide transmission map for the country, demonstrating substantial disease circulation in rural communities that have historically been underrepresented in case-based clinical surveillance records.
 Dengue virus infection represents a major global health burden across tropical and subtropical environments, producing severe clinical manifestations including dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome alongside extensive asymptomatic or self-limiting illness. In Timor-Leste, routine public health surveillance has historically depended upon case notifications from healthcare facilities, which systematically under-report true infection counts due to uneven healthcare-seeking behaviors, diagnostic barriers, and regional resource disparities. Because previous serological investigations in the country were limited to a single unrepresentative pilot study carried out between late 2018 and early 2019, the comprehensive geographic scope and underlying drivers of dengue transmission across rural and urban districts had remained uncharacterized until now.
 To evaluate transmission dynamics across diverse administrative landscapes, the investigative team deployed a three-stage cluster sampling design informed by World Health Organization cluster survey guidelines. Fieldwork executed between October 2021 and February 2023 randomly sampled households derived from the 2015 national housing census across 113 enumeration areas proportionate to municipal population sizes. Field teams successfully visited 102 enumeration areas across all thirteen administrative municipalities of Timor-Leste, achieving an enumeration area participation rate of 90.3 percent. Logistical barriers, including severe weather, impassable roads, time constraints, and staff illness, prevented sampling in eleven originally targeted enumeration areas.
 The serological dataset ultimately incorporated 4780 individuals residing within 1755 households across the 102 sampled enumeration areas, representing a household participation rate of 67.2 percent and an individual participation rate of 56.7 percent among enumerated occupants. The median participant age was 28 years with an inter-quartile range spanning 13 to 46 years, and female participants accounted for 59.2 percent of the sampled cohort. Demonstrating the representative demographic coverage of the survey across dispersed settlements, 73.0 percent of the participants resided in households classified as rural during the national census. Venous blood samples were collected via phlebotomy from consenting household occupants aged above one year, with target blood volumes stratified between children and adult cohorts.
 Collected serum specimens were transported under controlled refrigeration to the Laboratorio Nacional de Saude in Dili and evaluated using the commercial Panbio Indirect dengue IgG enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. This diagnostic assay measures human IgG antibodies directed against any dengue virus serotype, functioning as a marker of past lifetime infection rather than acute illness. Testing identified dengue IgG antibodies in 3931 individuals, yielding an overall raw seropositivity rate of 83.1 percent among participants. A small fraction of samples, comprising 57 individuals or 1.2 percent of the total dataset, fell into the manufacturer-defined equivocal index value range between 0.9 and 1.1 and were conservatively categorized as seronegative in the primary analysis.
 To translate binary cross-sectional antibody measures into an interpretable metric of exposure, researchers constructed a hierarchical Bayesian catalytic model. Operating under the epidemiological assumption of endemic equilibrium, the catalytic framework leverages participant age as an indicator of cumulative time at risk, parsing age-dependent seroprevalence curves into force-of-infection estimates. The statistical architecture represented force of infection on the logit scale, nesting individual probabilities within households and households within enumeration areas to account explicitly for intra-household clustering effects. In addition, the model directly estimated imperfect diagnostic accuracy, identifying an assay sensitivity of 99 percent and an assay specificity of 98 percent from the empirical data.
 The sero-catalytic analysis demonstrated intense spatial heterogeneity in transmission intensity across the surveyed enumeration areas, with median force-of-infection values varying by more than fifty-fold across different locales. Estimated median annual force of infection ranged from a low of 0.010, with a 95 percent credible interval spanning 0.005 to 0.018, in enumeration area 10104032 located in Fatubossa within Aileu municipality, to a high of 0.519, with a credible interval spanning 0.295 to 0.816, in enumeration area 40403012 in Goulolo within Bobonaro municipality. Enumeration areas situated in Bobonaro, Dili, Atauro Island, and Baucau exhibited the highest localized transmission metrics, whereas inland mountainous jurisdictions such as Aileu, Ainaro, and Ermera consistently demonstrated the lowest transmission values.
 To investigate the environmental and climatic determinants governing these spatial patterns, the researchers matched the enumeration area force-of-infection estimates with decadal gridded satellite observations spanning 2011 to 2022. Using stochastic partial differential equations within integrated nested Laplace approximations, the team fitted spatial regression models examining multi-year averages of temperature extremes, vapor pressure, accumulated rainfall, elevation, mid-infrared reflectance, and enhanced vegetation index. 
 Spatial regression analysis established that relative humidity exhibited a significant negative association with dengue virus force of infection. Across the joint posterior distributions, the median regression coefficient for relative humidity at minimum temperature was negative 0.96 with a 95 percent credible interval between negative 1.47 and negative 0.39, while relative humidity at maximum temperature yielded a median coefficient of negative 0.65 with a credible interval between negative 1.20 and negative 0.13. By contrast, enhanced vegetation index showed no statistically significant association with transmission intensity. The inverse relationship with relative humidity corresponds with local geographic gradients, where humidity peaks in elevated, cool mountain terrain but drops along warmer, highly populated coastal plains where mosquito proliferation and human biting rates are concentrated.
 Extrapolating model dynamics across all 2350 enumeration areas in Timor-Leste generated comprehensive nationwide predictions of transmission risk and expected pediatric immunity. The predictive models pinpointed the highest exposure rates along the northern and eastern coastlines, identifying prominent transmission hubs in urban centers such as Dili, Baucau, and Manatuto, as well as on Atauro Island. When aggregated to municipal boundaries, Atauro Island and Dili municipality displayed median predicted annual force-of-infection rates of 0.27 and 0.22, translating to anticipated median seroprevalence proportions at nine years of age of 91 percent and 86 percent, respectively. Municipalities including Lautem, Liquica, and Baucau similarly sustained force-of-infection values exceeding 0.15, corresponding to an expected nine-year-old seroprevalence above 74 percent.
 Conversely, high-altitude interior regions experienced substantially attenuated transmission intensities, with Aileu, Ainaro, and Ermera municipalities presenting median force-of-infection estimates below 0.05 and expected seroprevalence at age nine falling below 36 percent. The stark contrast between coastal lowlands and mountainous interiors underscores the role of local geography in shaping arboviral exposure. Furthermore, the identification of high transmission rates across rural sectors with negligible historic case reporting highlights the degree to which facility-based surveillance fails to detect widespread mild or subclinical infections, particularly where geographic isolation and limited clinical infrastructure restrict access to formal medical evaluations.
 The authors noted specific methodological limitations inherent to the survey design and historical datasets. Relying on sampling frames derived from the 2015 national housing census meant structural shifts in dwelling occupancy over the intervening six years could have introduced minor sampling discrepancies, though post-independence stabilization has reduced internal displacement. Additionally, assigning infection exposure to a participant’s current residence cannot fully capture infections acquired during travel between enumeration areas, and the time-constant modeling formulation does not estimate seasonal or interannual outbreak surges. Gridded environmental variables derived at spatial scales between one and five kilometers also necessitated spatial averaging across smaller enumeration areas.
 Despite these analytical caveats, the nationwide serosurvey establishes an essential baseline for contemporary public health decision-making in Timor-Leste. The reconstructed seroprevalence metrics at nine years of age provide specific empirical parameters mandated by World Health Organization frameworks to evaluate the programmatic introduction of dengue vaccines, such as TAK-003. Furthermore, the high-resolution mapping of transmission hotspots offers operational guidance for mosquito abatement initiatives and the targeted deployment of Wolbachia-infected mosquito release programs, ensuring vector control resources are directed toward communities bearing the highest cumulative infection burden.
